entry.title: Saving F* Words
entry.content:
Saving F* Words

Deploying NestJS + TypeORM + PostgreSQL to Supabase and Vercel without losing your mind.

Express wants a server. Guillermo Rauch wants a function.

And somehow, you’re supposed to make everyone happy.

Express was designed around a long-running process that listens on a port, handles requests, and stays alive. Vercel prefers serverless functions that can be invoked independently and scaled when needed.

TypeORM, meanwhile, would appreciate it if everyone stopped changing the rules halfway through initialization.

And you? You just wanted to deploy an API.

What could possibly go wrong?

Plenty, apparently.

This is a practical guide to deploying a NestJS application using Express, TypeORM, and PostgreSQL hosted on Supabase, with Vercel handling the application runtime.

We’ll cover the serverless adapter, database connections, migrations, environment variables, and the kind of deployment errors that make you question your career choices.

The examples assume NestJS 11, TypeORM, PostgreSQL, and a Vercel Node.js function. Exact runtime configuration may vary depending on the Vercel runtime and deployment setup you’re using, so treat the configuration as a starting point rather than a universal incantation.

Let’s save some F* words.

0. The architecture: what are we building?

The setup is straightforward on paper:

                    Client
                      |
                      v
             Vercel Serverless Function
                      |
                      v
               NestJS + Express
                      |
                      v
             Supabase Connection Pooler
                      |
                      v
                  PostgreSQL

The application runs as a serverless function on Vercel. PostgreSQL is hosted by Supabase, and the connection pooler helps manage database connections when multiple function instances are running.

Two principles explain most of the decisions in this guide:

  1. The application must work within the serverless execution model. You don’t simply start a permanent HTTP server and expect the platform to manage it like a traditional VM.
  2. Database migrations should run as a separate deployment step. Don’t let every application instance attempt to modify the database schema at startup.

That’s the whole idea.

The rest is making sure the implementation actually follows it.

1. Why deploying NestJS + Express to serverless hurts

A conventional NestJS application usually starts like this:

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);

  await app.listen(3000);
}

bootstrap();

This is perfectly reasonable for a traditional server, container, or virtual machine.

The process starts, binds to port 3000, and waits for incoming requests.

Vercel’s serverless execution model is different. The platform invokes a function to handle incoming requests. You generally don’t want your application entry point to call app.listen() and attempt to manage its own listening socket.

Instead, the platform handles the request lifecycle, and your function needs to expose a compatible request handler.

For an Express-based NestJS application, the ExpressAdapter gives us a way to connect the two.

1.1 Create a serverless entry point

Create api/index.ts:

import express from 'express';
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ExpressAdapter } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import { ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';

import { AppModule } from '../src/app.module';

export const config = {
  api: {
    bodyParser: false,
  },
};

let cachedServer: express.Express | undefined;

async function getServer(): Promise<express.Express> {
  if (!cachedServer) {
    const server = express();

    const app = await NestFactory.create(
      AppModule,
      new ExpressAdapter(server),
    );

    app.setGlobalPrefix('api');

    app.useGlobalPipes(
      new ValidationPipe({
        whitelist: true,
      }),
    );

    await app.init();

    cachedServer = server;
  }

  return cachedServer;
}

export default async (req, res) => {
  const server = await getServer();

  return server(req, res);
};

There are a few important details here.

app.init() instead of app.listen()

NestJS needs to initialize its modules, providers, middleware, and routes. app.init() performs application initialization without attempting to open a listening port.

The serverless platform is responsible for receiving the request.

Cache the initialized handler

The cachedServer variable lets the function reuse its initialized Express application when the same warm runtime instance handles subsequent requests.

That can avoid repeating the NestJS bootstrap process on every invocation handled by that instance.

However, don’t mistake this for a guarantee of a persistent process. Serverless platforms can create additional instances or replace existing ones whenever they need to.

Be careful with request body parsing

The bodyParser: false setting is relevant to Vercel’s compatible function configurations where the platform’s default body parser would otherwise consume the request stream before Express handles it.

This setting is not a universal requirement for every Vercel runtime. Check the runtime and request-handling behavior of your deployment before applying it blindly.

Because debugging an empty JSON body is fun exactly once.

1.2 Don’t duplicate your NestJS bootstrap configuration

There’s another problem hiding here.

Your local application may configure CORS, Helmet, validation pipes, interceptors, Swagger, and a global route prefix. If the serverless entry point initializes the application differently, your local and deployed environments can behave differently.

That’s a fantastic way to discover that your production API has a personality of its own.

Extract the shared setup into a reusable function.

For example, src/setup-app.ts:

import {
  INestApplication,
  ValidationPipe,
} from '@nestjs/common';

export function setupApp(app: INestApplication) {
  app.setGlobalPrefix('api');

  app.useGlobalPipes(
    new ValidationPipe({
      whitelist: true,
    }),
  );

  // Configure CORS, Helmet, interceptors,
  // filters, and other shared behavior here.

  return app;
}

Your conventional entry point can then use it:

import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';

import { AppModule } from './app.module';
import { setupApp } from './setup-app';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);

  setupApp(app);

  await app.listen(3000);
}

bootstrap();

And the serverless entry point can use the same configuration:

const app = await NestFactory.create(
  AppModule,
  new ExpressAdapter(server),
);

setupApp(app);

await app.init();

The goal is simple: share application configuration, but keep the runtime-specific startup logic separate.

1.3 Configure routing

A minimal vercel.json might look like this:

{
  "buildCommand": "npm run build",
  "functions": {
    "api/index.ts": {
      "maxDuration": 60,
      "memory": 1024
    }
  },
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/(.*)",
      "destination": "/api"
    }
  ]
}

This illustrates the intended routing and function resource configuration. Confirm that the options and rewrite behavior match the Vercel runtime and project configuration you’re actually using.

In particular, don’t assume that outputDirectory: "dist" is appropriate for every NestJS deployment. Vercel needs to build and package the function correctly; a directory containing your compiled NestJS application isn’t automatically a valid static output directory.

Also, make sure the rewrite behavior preserves the routes NestJS expects. If your application uses the global prefix api, verify that a request to /api/users reaches the correct NestJS route rather than accidentally producing /api/api/users.

Congratulations. You now have an application that can be initialized by a serverless function.

Only a few dozen more things can go wrong.

2. Prerequisites

Before continuing, make sure you have:

  • A NestJS project with TypeORM configured.
  • The PostgreSQL driver installed: pg.
  • A Supabase project with a PostgreSQL database.
  • A Vercel account and a working project configuration.
  • A compatible Node.js runtime.
  • A migration workflow that you can run independently of application startup.

If you already have a working NestJS application locally, that’s a good start.

If it doesn’t work locally, deploying it to another platform won’t magically improve the situation.

It will, however, give you more logs to read.

3. Set up PostgreSQL on Supabase

Create a project in Supabase and open the database connection settings.

Supabase provides connection details for connecting directly to PostgreSQL and for using its connection pooler, Supavisor.

For a serverless application, the pooler is worth considering because serverless platforms can run multiple function instances concurrently. Each instance may create its own database connection pool.

Without appropriate limits, the number of database connections can grow quickly.

For example:

20 function instances × 5 connections each = 100 connections

That is a simplified illustration, but it demonstrates the problem.

Now imagine each instance opens dozens of connections.

PostgreSQL will eventually remind you that connections are a finite resource.

3.1 Use the appropriate connection string

Supabase’s transaction-mode pooler commonly uses port 6543. Your exact hostname, username, and connection string should come from your Supabase dashboard.

A connection string may look similar to this:

postgresql://postgres.<project-ref>:<password>@<pooler-host>:6543/postgres

Use the actual values provided by Supabase rather than copying the placeholders.

Transaction pooling is useful for applications that open many short-lived connections, but it has limitations. Features that depend on a persistent database session may behave differently, so verify compatibility with your database driver and application.

Don’t assume that the direct connection and the pooler are interchangeable in every scenario.

3.2 Keep your database credentials private

Never commit your production connection string to Git.

Use environment variables or your platform’s secret-management mechanism. If a real credential has already been committed to a repository, removing it from the latest commit isn’t enough: rotate the credential.

The old value may still exist in Git history.

Yes, even if the repository is private.

Especially if the repository is private and you keep forgetting that other people can have access to it.

4. Database schema: migrations, not synchronize

TypeORM provides a convenient option:

synchronize: true

During local development, this can be useful for quickly iterating on an entity model.

In production, it’s not a substitute for a controlled schema migration strategy.

Your application schema is important data infrastructure. You should know which changes are being applied, when they’re applied, and whether they can safely be rolled back.

A safer production configuration is:

synchronize: false

Use migrations to create and modify database structures.

4.1 Run migrations separately

A typical deployment workflow looks like this:

1. Build and test the application
2. Run database migrations
3. Deploy the application
4. Verify the deployment

The migration command might look like:

DATABASE_URL='<your-database-url>' \
DATABASE_TYPE=postgres \
npm run migration:run

This is an example of passing environment variables to a command in a Unix-like shell. In a real project, use the configuration and scripts you’ve defined for your environment.

The important part is that migrations run as an explicit deployment step, not automatically in every serverless invocation.

Why?

Because multiple application instances shouldn’t independently race to change the schema during startup.

And because production database changes deserve a little more respect than a checkbox in a configuration file.

4.2 Configure TypeORM for the CLI

TypeORM’s CLI runs outside NestJS’s dependency injection system. A standalone DataSource configuration is therefore useful.

For example, src/database/data-source.ts:

import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export const AppDataSource = new DataSource({
  type: 'postgres',

  url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,

  host: process.env.DATABASE_HOST,

  port: process.env.DATABASE_PORT
    ? Number.parseInt(process.env.DATABASE_PORT, 10)
    : 5432,

  username: process.env.DATABASE_USERNAME,

  password: process.env.DATABASE_PASSWORD,

  database: process.env.DATABASE_NAME,

  synchronize: false,

  entities: [
    // Import or configure your entity classes here.
  ],

  migrations: [
    // Configure the migration files produced by your build.
  ],
});

If DATABASE_URL is set, make sure the remaining connection settings are handled consistently with your configuration and driver.

The migration paths must match your actual project structure and the files available to the CLI. TypeScript source paths and compiled JavaScript paths aren’t necessarily the same.

4.3 Configure TypeORM at runtime

NestJS can use TypeOrmModule and a configuration service to initialize the database connection.

A simplified example:

import {
  Injectable,
} from '@nestjs/common';

import {
  TypeOrmOptionsFactory,
  TypeOrmModuleOptions,
} from '@nestjs/typeorm';

import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';

@Injectable()
export class TypeOrmConfigService
  implements TypeOrmOptionsFactory
{
  constructor(
    private readonly configService: ConfigService,
  ) {}

  createTypeOrmOptions(): TypeOrmModuleOptions {
    return {
      type: 'postgres',

      url: this.configService.get<string>(
        'database.url',
      ),

      synchronize: false,

      entities: [
        // Explicit entity imports go here.
      ],

      migrations: [
        // Match your compiled migration files.
      ],

      extra: {
        max: 5,
      },
    };
  }
}

This is deliberately simplified. Adapt it to your project’s actual configuration schema, SSL requirements, migration setup, and entity list.

The max: 5 setting is an example, not a magic number. Choose a pool size based on the database connection budget, the number of concurrently running instances, and the workload.

The CLI and runtime configurations serve different purposes. Keeping them separate makes the behavior easier to understand and troubleshoot.

5. Configure environment variables in Vercel

Your application may work locally because your .env file contains everything it needs.

Vercel doesn’t automatically inherit your local environment.

You need to configure the variables in the appropriate Vercel project and deployment environment.

Typical variables include:

DATABASE_URL
DATABASE_SYNCHRONIZE
DATABASE_MAX_CONNECTIONS
DATABASE_SSL_ENABLED

AUTH_JWT_SECRET
AUTH_REFRESH_SECRET

APP_CORS_ORIGINS
THROTTLER_TTL
THROTTLER_LIMIT

The exact names depend on your application’s configuration.

For example, if your application reads database.url through NestJS’s ConfigService, verify that the configuration layer actually maps it to DATABASE_URL.

Adding a variable to Vercel doesn’t help if your application is looking for a completely different name.

5.1 Environment variable checklist

Variable Example Purpose
DATABASE_URL Supabase connection string Database connectivity
DATABASE_SYNCHRONIZE false Prevent automatic schema synchronization
DATABASE_MAX_CONNECTIONS 5 Limit connections per application instance
DATABASE_SSL_ENABLED true Enable TLS where required
AUTH_JWT_SECRET Generated secret Sign access tokens
AUTH_REFRESH_SECRET Separate generated secret Sign refresh tokens
APP_CORS_ORIGINS Your frontend origin Restrict permitted browser origins

Generate strong, unique secrets for authentication. Never reuse the same secret for unrelated purposes.

You can generate a random hexadecimal value locally with:

openssl rand -hex 32

Don’t put the generated value in your repository or paste it into a public issue.

5.2 Be careful with SSL settings

You may find examples that use:

ssl: {
  rejectUnauthorized: false,
}

This disables normal certificate verification. It can appear to solve a TLS connection error, but it also weakens protection against connecting to an untrusted endpoint.

Don’t copy it blindly into production.

Prefer a configuration that validates the server certificate correctly. If your environment has a certificate-chain problem, identify and fix the underlying issue where possible.

A successful connection is not automatically a secure connection.

That’s a lesson worth learning before someone else teaches it to you.

6. TypeORM in serverless: three details that can break everything

The database connection string is only part of the story. TypeORM also needs to discover entities, manage connections sensibly, and avoid relying on process state that may disappear.

6.1 Entity discovery: be careful with globs

A common TypeORM configuration uses a glob:

entities: [
  __dirname + '/**/*.entity{.ts,.js}',
]

This can work well in conventional Node.js deployments, depending on the build output and directory structure.

With serverless bundling, however, runtime file discovery and file inclusion can become more complicated. A bundler may not include files that are only discovered dynamically.

The result can be an error such as:

No metadata for "UserEntity" was found.

Or another variation of the classic:

Everything compiled successfully.
Why is production broken?

One approach is to import the entity classes explicitly:

import { UserEntity } from '../users/entities/user.entity';
import { ProductEntity } from '../products/entities/product.entity';

const entities = [
  UserEntity,
  ProductEntity,
];

Then configure TypeORM:

entities,

Explicit imports make dependencies easier for bundlers to detect and make the entity list easier to inspect.

They’re not mandatory in every deployment setup, but they’re a useful troubleshooting option when dynamic discovery fails.

6.2 Keep the connection pool under control

Consider this configuration:

extra: {
  max: 5,
},

For the PostgreSQL driver, this controls the maximum size of the connection pool passed to the underlying driver.

The correct value depends on your workload and connection limits.

If each function instance can open five connections and the platform starts twenty instances, the theoretical combined limit is one hundred connections.

That doesn’t mean all those connections will always be open, but it illustrates why per-instance settings matter.

Also, don’t assume that keeping the NestJS application initialized guarantees that a database connection will remain available forever. Network interruptions, database restarts, and runtime lifecycle changes still happen.

Design for reconnection and failure where appropriate.

6.3 Don’t rely on process memory for shared state

This is perfectly valid JavaScript:

const cache = new Map();

But it is not a distributed cache.

Each running function instance has its own memory. Another instance won’t automatically see the same map, and an instance can disappear at any time.

The same warning applies to:

  • In-memory rate limiters.
  • Sessions stored only in process memory.
  • Application caches that need to be shared.
  • Background jobs that must run reliably.
  • Cron-like tasks tied to a process that may stop.
  • WebSocket connections that require a persistent connection model.

If the data must be shared or survive beyond a particular instance, use an appropriate external service, such as Redis or PostgreSQL, or a dedicated job-processing system.

Serverless doesn’t mean you can’t use state.

It means you need to be explicit about where that state lives.

7. Deploy and verify

Before deploying, make sure your application builds successfully and your database schema is up to date.

A simplified workflow might look like this:

# 1. Run migrations from your deployment environment
npm run migration:run

# 2. Deploy
vercel --prod

The migration command assumes your CLI configuration and environment variables are already set up correctly. Don’t run it against production until you’ve verified the target database and reviewed the migrations.

After deployment, test the actual endpoints.

For example:

curl https://your-app.vercel.app/api

If your application exposes Swagger, you may also have endpoints such as:

https://your-app.vercel.app/docs
https://your-app.vercel.app/docs-json

These paths depend on your NestJS configuration. They won’t exist unless you’ve enabled and configured them.

Post-deployment checklist

  • The deployment completes successfully.
  • The application initializes without module or dependency errors.
  • A basic health endpoint responds as expected.
  • Database queries work against the intended Supabase project.
  • Authentication returns the expected tokens.
  • Validation and error handling behave correctly.
  • Swagger works, if enabled.
  • Logs don’t show repeated connection failures or missing entity metadata.
  • Production uses synchronize: false.
  • Database credentials and authentication secrets aren’t exposed.

Don’t stop at “Vercel says the deployment succeeded.”

A successful deployment means the platform deployed something. It doesn’t prove that your database works, your routes are correct, or your application can handle real requests.

Test the application, not the green checkmark.

8. Troubleshooting: the errors you’ll probably meet

Here’s a quick reference for some common problems.

Symptom Possible cause What to check
JSON request body is empty Request body was parsed or consumed before Express handles it Verify the Vercel runtime’s body-parsing behavior
EADDRINUSE or startup problems Application attempts to manage a listening socket in a function environment Review the entry point and use the appropriate initialization lifecycle
Repeated cold-start delays Application bootstrap runs repeatedly across invocations Reuse initialized state within warm instances where appropriate
too many clients Too many connections across instances or an unsuitable connection strategy Review pool sizes, concurrency, and Supabase pooler configuration
SSL connection errors TLS settings or certificate verification are incorrect Check the connection string and certificate configuration
No metadata for Entity was found Entity classes weren’t registered or included correctly Verify imports, entity configuration, and build output
Production schema differs from local Migrations weren’t applied or schema management is inconsistent Review migration status and disable automatic synchronization
Function timeout Request performs too much work or waits too long Profile the request, review platform limits, and move long jobs to a suitable worker
Missing templates or static files Required files weren’t included in the deployment bundle Inspect the generated function package and configure file inclusion if supported
Works locally, fails after deployment Different environment variables, paths, runtime behavior, or dependencies Compare the actual deployment configuration with local settings

The important word here is possible.

An error message is a clue, not a diagnosis. Check the actual logs and configuration before applying a fix from a blog post written by someone who has never seen your project.

Including me.

9. The minimum viable recipe

If you just want the checklist without the existential crisis, here it is.

  1. Create a PostgreSQL database in Supabase.
  2. Choose the appropriate database connection method; consider the Supabase pooler for serverless workloads.
  3. Configure NestJS to initialize correctly in the Vercel runtime.
  4. Avoid starting a conventional listening server inside a function entry point unless the runtime explicitly requires that model.
  5. Share your NestJS configuration between local and serverless entry points.
  6. Set synchronize: false in production.
  7. Run migrations as a separate deployment step.
  8. Configure the database URL, authentication secrets, and other environment variables in Vercel.
  9. Register entities explicitly if dynamic discovery causes bundling problems.
  10. Keep connection pools appropriately small and account for concurrent function instances.
  11. Verify TLS configuration rather than blindly disabling certificate verification.
  12. Test the deployed API, database connectivity, authentication, and logs.

That’s the technical part.

The real challenge is understanding the difference between a conventional Node.js server and a serverless function. Once that clicks, most of the configuration choices become easier to explain.

Not necessarily easier to debug.

Let’s not get carried away.

10. Why Vercel Instead of Render?

Was Vercel the only reasonable choice? No.

Would another hosting platform have made some parts of this setup simpler? Quite possibly.

Did I choose Vercel partly because I wanted to try it and see what all the fuss was about?

Absolutely.

Sometimes the best reason to try a technology is curiosity. Sometimes it’s the ecosystem. Sometimes you want to learn a deployment model you’ve never used before.

And sometimes everybody on the internet seems to be using a platform, and you don’t want to be the only person at the party who brought a virtual machine.

There’s nothing wrong with experimenting. Just be honest about the trade-offs.

Vercel’s serverless model can be convenient, but it also introduces constraints around execution time, process lifecycle, connection management, and background work. A conventional application host may offer a simpler model for a long-running NestJS API.

Choose the platform that fits your application, not the one with the most fashionable dashboard.

Or don’t.

I’m not your manager.

Final thoughts

Express expects a server.

Vercel expects a function.

TypeORM expects its entities to exist.

PostgreSQL expects you not to open an unreasonable number of connections.

And you expect npm run build to be the end of your problems.

One of those expectations is clearly unrealistic.

The good news is that NestJS, TypeORM, Supabase, and Vercel can work together when the runtime, database configuration, and deployment process are designed with their constraints in mind.

The less good news is that you’ll probably discover at least one configuration issue that wasn’t mentioned in this article.

When you do, document it.

Future you will be grateful. Other developers might be grateful, too.

And if nothing else, you’ll have one more reason to write a blog post.

Saving F* Words: because sometimes the most valuable thing a developer can save isn’t a line of code.

It’s an afternoon of debugging.

And a few thousand swear words.
entry.summary: A practical guide to deploying NestJS, TypeORM, and PostgreSQL on Supabase and Vercel, with fewer surprises and hopefully fewer swear words.

entry.title: Why I Start 20 Projects and Finish 3 (and Why That’s Okay)

link.title: Why I Start 20 Projects and Finish 3 (and Why That’s Okay)

entry.content:
I have a problem. It’s not serious, it doesn’t hurt, but it’s there, like a zombie process nobody killed: accumulating GitHub repositories that I open every now and then just to remind myself they exist and feel a perfectly manageable pang of guilt.

The problem is this: I start projects the way I breathe, without thinking, without asking for permission. And I finish, at best, one out of every six. The other five remain in a state that a cardiologist would describe as “stable but unconscious.”

So, to keep this from being abstract, here’s a representative sample of the zoo I currently have active:

  • A reverse proxy built from scratch with net/http, without any libraries, “to understand how it really works” (spoiler: I still don’t fully understand it, but after three months of saying “it’s almost done,” I can’t exactly admit it to anyone now).

  • A P2P streaming system over WebRTC DataChannels with peer selection based on scoring, because apparently what my life was missing was reinventing BitTorrent, but worse, and without any users.

  • An app like Rocksmith, but with chords synchronized over YouTube videos.

  • A private BitTorrent tracker with a Discord bot next to it, because a big project never comes alone, it comes with children.

  • A vinyl price scraper, so I can complain about how expensive records are and which seller has them cheaper, obviously without actually buying anything.

  • An events and concerts scraper, so I can make myself miserable and see how expensive it is to go see that indie band I only know and that costs more than 100 USD.

And that’s what I can remember off the top of my head. I’m probably missing a few. Being almost 40 doesn’t come alone, just like my Alzheimer’s.

Why me?

No idea. I guess for a long time I thought it was a lack of discipline. Now it’s more about not having enough time, and whenever I do have some free time, wanting to do 40 things at the same time. But basically, I have a brain that confuses “interest” with “lifelong commitment” every time a new shiny problem appears.

The dopamine of a new project isn’t in finishing it. It’s in the first week, when everything is still a promise: when the problem is purely conceptual and you haven’t yet hit the horrifying detail that’s going to make you hate the project three weeks later. Starting a project is the cheapest, nicest part and, let’s be honest, the only part my brain actually feels like paying for.

Then there’s the contrast. My day-to-day job is fintech: Lambdas, Step Functions, DynamoDB, YAML at two in the morning. It’s a job I like, but it lives in the world of “solving someone else’s business problem.” Personal projects are my playground — that’s where my real interest in streaming and media engineering lives, which has absolutely nothing to do with what the company I work for gets paid for. So when I start a new project in this area, technically I’m not avoiding anything — I’m going back to something I actually enjoy. The problem is that I have a special and obsessive interest in too many things at once, and absolutely no ability to say “no, not this week.”

And finally, there’s pure technical curiosity. I’ve always had that curiosity about how certain things were built, which is very different from the need to actually finish something. Sometimes what I want isn’t “a finished product for the world,” I just want to know how it works under the hood, down to the last detail, obsessively. Once I understand the mechanism, my motivation to polish it and make it nice for other humans falls off a cliff like a service nobody asked for.

The Last of Us

It’s not all a graveyard. Some projects actually reached a usable or semi-zombie state, and looking back, they have something in common: they were small, had a visible finish line, or solved something I personally needed in an urgent way.

The vinyl price scraper is the perfect example: it was born out of a real and recurring pain (not knowing whether the record I want is actually a good deal or whether someone is ripping me off), had a ridiculously limited scope, and the day it worked, it worked. It didn’t need to be pretty or scalable, it just needed to warn me before I spent money I didn’t have on an overpriced record.

The pattern repeats: when a project is born from “I need to solve this for myself, right now, this week,” it tends to survive. When it is born from “hey, wouldn’t it be cool if I could make something work like this?” my brain loses interest as soon as it understands the underlying problem, and the rest becomes an eternal theoretical exercise.

Now, “survive” has a particular definition in my dictionary, because scrapers have their own problem, and the problem is me: I’m cheap as hell. I’m not going to pay for a VPS, an instance, or anything with a recurring monthly cost for something that isn’t sellable, has no other users, and that I only use a couple of times a month so I don’t buy an overpriced vinyl or find out too late about a show that’s already sold out. So instead of living in the cloud like it’s supposed to, these scrapers run as cron jobs on some old Linux PC.

Plants vs. Zombies

Then there’s the rest. The reverse proxy that I got halfway through understanding. The P2P system that has a peer-scoring architecture more elaborate than some projects that actually charge money and have investors. The concert scraper that was supposed to notify me about every show in the country and that, the last time I looked at it, was notifying me about a show that had happened two months earlier. Things I started, learned a lot from, and then abandoned with the same tranquility with which you leave a dirty plate “for later.”

I didn’t delete them. They’re still there, like a stuffed dog in the living room. I learned something from each of them — even if it’s just “this was harder than I thought” or, more honestly, “what I really wanted was to understand it, not have it.”

Question!

And why don’t you make some of those side projects into tutorials or courses, so you can learn something with less drama?

Because I’m not interested in pre-chewed challenges. I like the challenge itself, not the feeling of completing a checklist that someone else already solved for me. A side project cloned from a tutorial is like having the same duplicate sticker that millions of developers on the internet have: clone Netflix number 4,582, todo app number 9,213. All lined up on the same shelf, indistinguishable from one another, like the Buzz Lightyear joke in Toy Story when he realizes he’s just another toy from an entire production line. I’d rather have my original failures, thanks.

The Final Cut

I don’t know if this can be cured. Again, it’s not just a lack of discipline. If I ever manage to finish everything I start, it’ll be because I’ve run out of ideas, or because I finally decided to blame television or TikTok for my lack of imagination. If I stumble across an interesting technical problem tomorrow, I’ll most likely create a new repository instead of going back and finishing one of the six I already have open.

The point isn’t to end this post with a promise that someday I’ll finish everything — I don’t even have the excuse of saying “I’ll finish it by the end of the year.” It’s September, this is pure and genuine off-season overconfidence. I’ve already made a similar promise before, and we all know how that ended — just like the “Stuff’s Coming (Eventually)” post, followed by months of radio silence.

I’m simply going to accept that I’m someone who collects the beginnings of projects with the same obsession with which I collect vinyl records: I don’t always listen to them all the way through, but I need to own them.

entry.title: How I Broke Better Player (Without Actually Replacing It)

link.title: How I Broke Better Player (Without Actually Replacing It)

entry.content:
I started the weekend with a simple idea:

“I’ll tweak an open source IPTV Flutter project a bit and call it a day.”

Yeah… no.

The project was using Better Player.
At first glance, everything looked fine:

  • streams were playing
  • DASH (.mpd) worked
  • even DRM (ClearKey) was supported

So naturally, I assumed the hard parts were already solved.

They weren’t.

The First Problem

The stream had multiple audio tracks.

The player had… one.

No selector.
No API.
No indication that multiple tracks even existed.

Just:

“Here’s your audio. Enjoy.”

Trying Alternatives (Spoiler: Didn’t Work)

First stop: video_player.

  • simple
  • official
  • useless for this case

No real support for:

  • advanced DASH
  • DRM
  • track selection

Then I tried media_kit.

This one looked promising:

  • multiple audio tracks ✔️
  • subtitles ✔️
  • clean API ✔️

But then:

DRM: nope.

And not “kind of no”.
More like:

“This is not part of the stack.”

Because on Android, DRM lives in a completely different world.

The Realization

At that point it became obvious:

If I want proper DASH + DRM, I’m using ExoPlayer.

And Better Player… was already using it.

So the question changed from:

“Which library should I use?”

to:

“What is this library hiding from me?”

The Hack (Yes, Reflection)

val pluginClass = Class.forName("com.sarthak.better_player_enhanced.BetterPlayerPlugin")
val videoPlayersField = pluginClass.getDeclaredField("videoPlayers")
videoPlayersField.isAccessible = true

val videoPlayers = videoPlayersField.get(pluginInstance) as LongSparseArray<Any>
val betterPlayer = videoPlayers[textureId]

val exoPlayerField = betterPlayer.javaClass.getDeclaredField("exoPlayer")
exoPlayerField.isAccessible = true

val exoPlayer = exoPlayerField.get(betterPlayer) as ExoPlayer

Yes, it’s reflection.
Yes, it’s ugly.
Yes, it works.

Suddenly… Audio Tracks Exist

Once I had the real ExoPlayer:

exoPlayer.currentTracks.groups
    .filter { it.type == C.TRACK_TYPE_AUDIO }

And just like that:

👉 all audio tracks showed up

They were always there. Better Player just didn’t expose them.

Selecting one was straightforward:

trackSelector.parameters = trackSelector.buildUponParameters()
    .setOverrideForType(
        TrackSelectionOverride(group.mediaTrackGroup, 0)
    )
    .build()

Done.

Wiring It Through MainActivity

I exposed this through a MethodChannel.

Now Flutter can:

  • get audio tracks
  • get subtitle tracks
  • select tracks
  • listen for subtitle cues

Example:

when (call.method) {

    "getAudioTracks" -> {
        val tracks = exoPlayer.currentTracks.groups
            .filter { it.type == C.TRACK_TYPE_AUDIO }
            .mapIndexed { i, group ->
                val fmt = group.getTrackFormat(0)
                mapOf(
                    "groupIndex" to i,
                    "language" to (fmt.language ?: "und"),
                    "label" to (fmt.label ?: "Audio $i")
                )
            }
        result.success(tracks)
    }

    "selectAudioTrack" -> {
        val groupIndex = call.argument<Int>("groupIndex")!!
        val group = audioGroups[groupIndex]

        trackSelector.parameters = trackSelector.buildUponParameters()
            .setOverrideForType(
                TrackSelectionOverride(group.mediaTrackGroup, 0)
            )
            .build()

        result.success(null)
    }
}

Flutter Side (Still Using Better Player)

Here’s the funny part:

I didn’t remove Better Player.

_betterPlayerController = BetterPlayerController(config);

_betterPlayerController!.setupDataSource(
  BetterPlayerDataSource(
    BetterPlayerDataSourceType.network,
    url,
    videoFormat: BetterPlayerVideoFormat.dash,
    drmConfiguration: BetterPlayerDrmConfiguration(
      drmType: BetterPlayerDrmType.clearKey,
      clearKey: jwk,
    ),
  ),
);

It still handles:

  • rendering
  • lifecycle
  • texture management

But now I can fetch native tracks:

final audios = await _betterPlayerController!.getNativeAudioTracks();
final subs = await _betterPlayerController!.getNativeSubtitleTracks();

And render them:

ListTile(
  title: Text(track['label']),
  onTap: () {
    _betterPlayerController!
        .selectNativeAudioTrack(track['groupIndex']);
  },
)

Subtitles (Custom Rendering)

Better Player wasn’t handling subtitles well either.

So I listened directly from ExoPlayer:

override fun onCues(cueGroup: CueGroup) {
    val text = cueGroup.cues
        .mapNotNull { it.text?.toString() }
        .joinToString("\n")

    channel.invokeMethod("onSubtitleCue", text)
}

Then rendered them in Flutter:

if (_subtitlesActive && _currentSubtitle.isNotEmpty)
  Positioned(
    bottom: 60,
    child: Text(_currentSubtitle),
  )

What This Became

Without really planning it, I ended up with:

Flutter UI
   ↓
Better Player (render + lifecycle)
   ↓
ExoPlayer (actual control)

The Takeaway

I didn’t:

  • switch frameworks
  • rewrite everything in Kotlin
  • abandon Flutter

I just:

stopped treating the plugin as a black box

Better Player isn’t bad. But its abstraction:

  • hides too much
  • simplifies too aggressively
  • breaks down in complex scenarios

Conclusion

Sometimes the problem isn’t the tool.

It’s how much of it you’re allowed to see.

And when you need more:

you either switch tools…
or go deeper.

I went deeper.

So far… it works 😄

The Result

  • Multi-audio ✔️
  • Subtitles ✔️
  • DRM ✔️

Without replacing Better Player.

entry.title: Is It Already Dead? Or Can Something Be Saved?

link.title: Is It Already Dead? Or Can Something Be Saved?

entry.content:
In 2011, I walked into a job interview for a developer position.
When they asked if I knew Progress, I said yes — thinking they meant PostgreSQL.

They didn’t.
It wasn’t.
And that misunderstanding ended up shaping an entire chapter of my career.

What started as confusion became my primary development environment for years. While the tech world talked about open stacks, huge communities, and fast-moving ecosystems, I stepped into a parallel universe where almost everything revolved around a single platform, a single vendor, and a very particular way of thinking about software.

For a long time, I saw it as a disadvantage. Today, I see it as an uncomfortable but important part of how I grew as an engineer.

The Parallel World

Working with Progress OpenEdge wasn’t just using a different database or language. It meant entering a complete ecosystem — fairly closed, with its own tools, rules, and philosophy.

While the outside world was discussing:

  • REST APIs
  • microservices
  • open-source communities
  • stacks evolving every year

I was working with:

  • ABL
  • AppServers
  • a database tightly coupled to the language
  • and a much smaller, quieter community

The constant feeling was being outside the global tech conversation. Not because we weren’t building real systems — we were — but because we were doing it on an island.

The Frustration (and What Wasn’t Said)

Some things weighed heavily:

  • Documentation that was hard to navigate
  • A small community to learn from
  • Strong vendor lock-in
  • Difficulty translating that experience into the broader job market
  • A pace of evolution that didn’t match what was happening outside

This wasn’t just a technical issue. It was professional.
You felt like you were growing — but along an axis the rest of the industry barely noticed.

For years, I thought the problem was the technology itself.

Eventually, I realized it wasn’t that simple.

The Uncomfortable Part to Admit

ABL had good ideas.

It took me years to say that without resistance.

Statements like:

  • FOR EACH
  • FIND FIRST
  • record buffers
  • the tight integration between business logic and data access

were incredibly comfortable for certain types of applications. For record-oriented business logic, they often felt more natural and expressive than writing raw SQL mixed with another language.

It wasn’t technical incompetence.
It was a different mental model.

The problem wasn’t the paradigm.

The problem was isolation.

It Didn’t Die for Being Useless — It Drifted Away

Over time, I noticed something: many technologies don’t disappear because they’re bad. They fade because they no longer belong to the ecosystem where the industry moves.

Progress OpenEdge became trapped in:

  • a small community
  • strong vendor dependency
  • limited integration with the open world
  • difficulty evolving at the pace of the broader market

That doesn’t invalidate the ideas.
But it does affect survival.

This wasn’t a technical collapse.
It was an ecosystem and cultural mismatch.

The Transition

When I started working with other technologies — Node, cloud platforms, modern architectures — I didn’t stop comparing everything to what I had seen in ABL.

But the tone changed. It wasn’t frustration anymore. It was curiosity:

What if these ideas existed in an open environment?
What if a data-oriented language model wasn’t tied to a single vendor?

I realized something important:
I didn’t want to escape what I had learned. I wanted to reinterpret it.

LiteABL: Not a Replacement, but Closure

Building a PoC runtime inspired by ABL ideas didn’t come from anger or nostalgia. It came from technical curiosity and a personal need for closure.

It’s not a competitor.
It’s not a replacement.
It’s not a commercial product.

It’s a question written in code.

If you’re curious, the experiment lives here:
👉 https://github.com/osgioia/liteabl/

Can we keep the ideas without carrying the closed ecosystem around them?

For me, this project isn’t the beginning of something. It’s the end of something.

Closing a Chapter

Progress was my technical school, even when I wanted to leave it. It forced me to think differently, to understand models that weren’t trendy, to solve problems in a context I didn’t choose but that still shaped me.

Today, I don’t want to stay there.
But I also don’t want to pretend it didn’t matter.

That misunderstanding in a 2011 interview ended up defining years of my professional life. LiteABL isn’t a rebellion against that past. It’s my way of closing the cycle while understanding everything that happened along the way.

Maybe the product is in decline.
But the ideas were never worthless.

And I carried some of them with me.

entry.title: React Portfolio + Jekyll Blog: Linking Them with GitHub Actions

link.title: React Portfolio + Jekyll Blog: Linking Them with GitHub Actions

entry.content:
Maintaining a personal portfolio is often a dilemma: you want the flexibility of React to create an interactive and modern landing page, but for writing content, nothing beats the simplicity of a Markdown-based static site generator like Jekyll.

Why choose one when you can have both? In this post, I’ll show you how I configured my site so that the portfolio lives at the root (/) and the blog in a sub-path (/blog), using GitHub Actions to make the magic happen on its own.

The Project Structure

The biggest challenge was organizing the files so they wouldn’t overlap. My structure looks like this:

.
├── .github/workflows/   <-- Where the CI/CD configuration lives
├── blog/                <-- The entire Jekyll site
│   ├── _posts/
│   ├── _config.yml
│   └── index.md
├── src/                 <-- React source code (living at the root)
├── public/              <-- React static assets
├── package.json         <-- React dependencies
└── tailwind.config.js

Configuring Jekyll for a Sub-path

For Jekyll to know it won’t be at the root of the domain, we need to adjust the _config.yml. This is vital so that the generated file paths don’t break:

# blog/_config.yml
title: My Blog
baseurl: "/blog" # <--- Vital to serve from my-domain.com/blog
url: "https://osgioia.dev"

This ensures that all internal links and Jekyll CSS files are correctly served from /blog/assets/....

The Magic: GitHub Actions

This is where the real integration happens. We need a workflow that detects what changed and builds only what’s necessary.

1. Smart Change Detection

We don’t want to build React if we only wrote a Markdown post. We use a bash script in the workflow to detect affected directories:

- name: Check for changes
  id: changes
  run: |
    DIFF_OUTPUT="$(git diff --name-only $ $)"
    
    if echo "$DIFF_OUTPUT" | grep -E '^(src/|public/|package\.json)' > /dev/null; then
      echo "react_changed=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
    fi

    if echo "$DIFF_OUTPUT" | grep -E '^blog/' > /dev/null; then
      echo "blog_changed=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
    fi

2. Conditional Builds

Then, we use that output to run build steps only when needed:

# React Build (only if frontend changed)
- name: Build React portfolio
  if: steps.changes.outputs.react_changed == 'true'
  run: |
    npm ci
    npm run build

# Jekyll Build (only if blog changed)
- name: Build Jekyll blog
  if: steps.changes.outputs.blog_changed == 'true'
  run: |
    cd blog
    bundle exec jekyll build --destination ../_site/blog

3. Merging the Sites

The final step is to merge both results into a single _site folder that GitHub Pages can serve:

- name: Prepare deployment directory
  run: |
    mkdir -p _site
    
    # Copy React build (goes to the root /)
    if [ -d "build" ]; then
      cp -r build/* _site/
    fi

    # The Jekyll build was already done inside _site/blog/
    # so the final structure is perfect.

Why This Solution?

  • React for UX: My landing page uses animations and dynamic components.
  • Jekyll for SEO: Blog posts are pure static HTML, perfect for indexing.
  • Zero Cost: The best part is that all of this is 100% free. GitHub Pages hosts the site at no cost, and GitHub Actions gives us free execution minutes to build the code every time we push.

I hope this technical breakdown helps you set up your own “Frankenstein” of web technologies without spending a single cent!
entry.summary: Learn how to set up a hybrid site with React for your landing page and Jekyll for your blog, all automatically deployed to a single GitHub Pages URL.

entry.title: Old-School Devs Aren’t Outdated — They’re Just Underrated

link.title: Old-School Devs Aren’t Outdated — They’re Just Underrated

entry.content:
We’ve all heard it: “Knowing COBOL or VB6 doesn’t count anymore.”

Funny thing is, people who say that usually forget that half the world still runs on those technologies — banks, governments, insurance systems, healthcare, all of it.
And behind that code are devs who’ve been solving real-world problems for decades, keeping critical systems alive while the rest of us argue about which JavaScript framework is slightly less awful this year.

They’re not outdated. They’re battle-tested.

The Bootcamp Paradox

Nothing against bootcamps — they open doors for a lot of people.
The issue is how the industry glorifies “modern stacks” while ignoring experience that actually matters.

A junior who knows React and a bit of Node.js might get more interviews than a dev who spent 20 years optimizing financial systems in COBOL.
That’s not logic — that’s marketing.

And here’s the twist: the learning curve for an old-school dev picking up modern tech is usually shorter.
They already understand logic, databases, concurrency, and performance.
They’ve debugged disasters at 3 AM with no Stack Overflow link to save them.
Learning a new syntax? That’s the easy part.

Reinventing the Wheel (Because You Had To)

What most people don’t realize is that legacy devs had to reinvent everything.
In environments like COBOL or Progress 4GL, there were no libraries, no frameworks, no “npm install something-that-solves-it-for-me”.

If you needed to parse a JSON file, you couldn’t just do import json.
You had to build the damn parser yourself.

That teaches a different mindset — you start thinking like an engineer, not just a code implementer.
You learn to build tools, not just use them.

So when those same devs jump into Node.js, Go, or Python, they adapt fast — because they already understand how things work under the hood.

The Bottom Line

Software changes every year, but fundamentals don’t.
A dev who’s survived multiple tech eras and still stays curious is worth a lot — not for nostalgia, but for what it represents:
technical resilience and adaptability.

Those are things no bootcamp can teach in three months.
entry.summary: Hot take: old-school devs could outlearn most bootcamp grads before lunch — and still have time to fix production.

entry.title: Stuff’s Coming (Eventually)
entry.content:
We’ve all heard it: “Big things coming soon!”

Usually said by your friend’s indie band that’s been promising a new EP since 2019. Well… welcome to the software version of that.

This blog exists mostly so I can tell myself I’m working on “content” while doing absolutely nothing about it for weeks. But hey — baby steps. At least I set up Jekyll and deployed it. That counts as productivity™.

A Little Disclaimer

Everything I write here is heavily altered to protect the innocent (and the legally questionable). Names of companies, products, or people will either be changed or conveniently forgotten — not because I’m polite, but because lawsuits are expensive and I’m not AWS.

What To Expect (Maybe)

Think of this blog as a mix of:

  • Tech stuff I found cool, confusing, or downright stupid
  • Personal war stories from working in cloud and backend development
  • The occasional meme in disguise as a “best practice”

Will I post regularly? Who knows.
Will it be useful? Probably.
Will it be sarcastic? Absolutely.

So yeah… enjoy it. Or don’t. I’m not your manager.
entry.summary: You know that thing indie bands always say before ghosting for 8 months? Yeah, that.
